3: Exclaimed: “My Master, now declare to me What people these are, and if all were clerks, These shaven crowns upon the left of us.”
8: And he to me: “All of them were asquint In intellect in the first life, so much That there with measure they no spending made.
12: Clearly enough their voices bark it forth, Whene’er they reach the two points of the circle, Where sunders them the opposite defect.
17: Clerks those were who no hairy covering Have on the head, and Popes and Cardinals, In whom doth Avarice practise its excess.”
22: And I: “My Master, among such as these I ought forsooth to recognise some few, Who were infected with these maladies.”
26: And he to me: “Vain thought thou entertainest; The undiscerning life which made them sordid Now makes them unto all discernment dim.
30: Forever shall they come to these two buttings; These from the sepulchre shall rise again With the fist closed, and these with tresses shorn.
35: Ill giving and ill keeping the fair world Have ta’en from them, and placed them in this scuffle; Whate’er it be, no words adorn I for it.
40: Now canst thou, Son, behold the transient farce Of goods that are committed unto Fortune, For which the human race each other buffet;
44: For all the gold that is beneath the moon, Or ever has been, of these weary souls Could never make a single one repose.”
48: “Master,” I said to him, “now tell me also What is this Fortune which thou speakest of, That has the world’s goods so within its clutches?”
52: And he to me: “O creatures imbecile, What ignorance is this which doth beset you? Now will I have thee learn my judgment of her.
57: He whose omniscience everything transcends The heavens created, and gave who should guide them, That every part to every part may shine,
62: Distributing the light in equal measure; He in like manner to the mundane splendours Ordained a general ministress and guide,
66: That she might change at times the empty treasures From race to race, from one blood to another, Beyond resistance of all human wisdom.
71: Therefore one people triumphs, and another Languishes, in pursuance of her judgment, Which hidden is, as in the grass a serpent.
76: Your knowledge has no counterstand against her; She makes provision, judges, and pursues Her governance, as theirs the other gods.
81: Her permutations have not any truce; Necessity makes her precipitate, So often cometh who his turn obtains.
85: And this is she who is so crucified Even by those who ought to give her praise, Giving her blame amiss, and bad repute.
89: But she is blissful, and she hears it not; Among the other primal creatures gladsome She turns her sphere, and blissful she rejoices.
94: Let us descend now unto greater woe; Already sinks each star that was ascending When I set out, and loitering is forbidden.”
99: We crossed the circle to the other bank, Near to a fount that boils, and pours itself Along a gully that runs out of it.
103: The water was more sombre far than perse; And we, in company with the dusky waves, Made entrance downward by a path uncouth.
108: A marsh it makes, which has the name of Styx, This tristful brooklet, when it has descended Down to the foot of the malign gray shores.
114: And I, who stood intent upon beholding, Saw people mud-besprent in that lagoon, All of them naked and with angry look.
118: They smote each other not alone with hands, But with the head and with the breast and feet, Tearing each other piecemeal with their teeth.
123: Said the good Master: “Son, thou now beholdest The souls of those whom anger overcame; And likewise I would have thee know for certain
128: Beneath the water people are who sigh And make this water bubble at the surface, As the eye tells thee wheresoe’er it turns.
137: Fixed in the mire they say, ‘We sullen were In the sweet air, which by the sun is gladdened, Bearing within ourselves the sluggish reek;
138: Now we are sullen in this sable mire.’ This hymn do they keep gurgling in their throats, For with unbroken words they cannot say it.”
139:
Thus we went circling round the filthy fen A great arc ’twixt the dry bank and the swamp, With eyes turned unto those who gorge the mire;

Unto the foot of a tower we came at last.
144:
Inferno: Canto VIII

I say, continuing, that long before We to the foot of that high tower had come, Our eyes went upward to the summit of it,
146: By reason of two flamelets we saw placed there, And from afar another answer them, So far, that hardly could the eye attain it.
147: And, to the sea of all discernment turned, I said: “What sayeth this, and what respondeth That other fire? and who are they that made it?”
149: And he to me: “Across the turbid waves What is expected thou canst now discern, If reek of the morass conceal it not.”
152: Cord never shot an arrow from itself That sped away athwart the air so swift, As I beheld a very little boat
153: Come o’er the water tow’rds us at that moment, Under the guidance of a single pilot, Who shouted, “Now art thou arrived, fell soul?”
157: “Phlegyas, Phlegyas, thou criest out in vain For this once,” said my Lord; “thou shalt not have us Longer than in the passing of the slough.”
